scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.

The record is a geographic area spanning several regimes and continuing peoples. French Guiana is not the independent country Guyana. South America corrects the imported regional classification. The researched summary replaces an introduction that also placed the territory in the West Indies. Imported Wikipedia text and its attribution remain unchanged in the generated source file.

The Chemin Saint-Louis account was read in the indexed full page 19 of Inrap’s 2008 report. Direct PDF access returned a challenge. Its approximate 50 to 220 CE occupation is not first human settlement, and the report’s then-unresolved pottery classification is not presented as a newly established ethnic group. Black soil is not automatically proof of a particular farming technique. No artifact image was claimed as inspected.

McKey and colleagues’ 2010 paper was read through the Smithsonian repository PDF, pages 2 and 3. Field alignments and drainage purposes are interpretations. Calibrated dates at Sable Blanc, K-VIII and Bois Diable support an early-second-millennium context; the broad 1000 to 1500 phase does not equate every archaeological culture, field or deposit. Soil phytoliths and starch on ceramic griddles are explicitly distinguished. The Suriname wooden shovel is not relocated to French Guiana. No dietary percentages, population estimate or recipe is inferred.

LandArc’s original research summary was read through the forge sections. The 1997 and 2006 dates are excavation campaigns, not dates of manufacture. Unfinished hoe blades supply evidence of production stages. The page has slightly inconsistent totals, so no aggregate artifact count is used. A proposed Indigenous identity for a silver earring’s wearer and its uniqueness claim are omitted. Tools recovered at a plantation do not identify their makers or imply free labour.

The opening paragraph of Houle-Wierzbicki and Le Roux’s Karapa 4 report was read in indexed text. Its 1668 to 1764 span describes Jesuit management, not an exact deposition date for all artifacts or immediate disappearance of the site. Its admiration for colonial administrators is not adopted; the card foregrounds enslaved labour and the limits of identifying particular workers.

Cazelles’ Karapa 2 article was downloaded from Manioc and its printed pages 14 and 15 read in extracted text. The PDF presents two printed pages per spread. Kitchen pottery, masonry potager and bread oven are reported finds. The hospital’s proximity to the kitchen is distinguished from the author’s conditional interpretation about historical beliefs in warmth. No clinical outcome, modern treatment recommendation or praise of enslavers is inferred. Other parts of the issue were not used to invent household habits.

The Manioc database introduction was read. Its 1848 to 1853 newly freed registers are distinguished from additional records planned for later integration. Searchable names, places, age and occupation do not make a full biography; no living person or personal record was looked up or reproduced. The text avoids treating administrative categories as the entirety of someone’s identity.

Aluku heritage houses are described for Boniville and Loka, using the park’s account of consultation and the restoration project. Timber, gabled roofs and carved koppo are not universal or timeless housing traits. The apprenticeship structure is documented; proposed functions or later completion of every renovation are not assumed.

The Antecume Pata workshop paragraph is dated 2017, the year of the described participation. The article’s account of 2015 initiation is not a claim that organized learning began then among Wayana or Apalaï people. The separate planned Cayodé programme is not represented as completed. Living Indigenous people are not described as vanished or as one undifferentiated culture.

The carnival inventory was submitted on October 13, 2017 and included in the national inventory that year. Its costume and galette sections were read. The card does not claim UNESCO inscription, uniform participation, an unchanging tradition, or that children attend the adult masked dances. Gossip about relationships, homophobic commentary, speculative theories of fertility and a claim that alcoholic punch prevents chills are excluded. The perfume detail is documented; the detective and hosting lines are light commentary.

CNES’s sounding-rocket history was read in full. April 9, 1968 was the first launch from the Guiana Space Centre. The radio-equipped payload recovery was a test, not a crewed flight or satellite launch. No current launch schedule, ownership of every European rocket or assumption that all residents benefited equally is added.

The ANOM research guide is used for broad settlement and penal-institution chronology, not to certify territorial boundaries. Its count of prisoners and apparent implication of continuous transportation through 1953 were not adopted. The 1852 to 1946 period labels the colonial administrative setting; it does not claim all prisons closed in 1946.

The Fondation pour la mémoire de l’esclavage account distinguishes Guyane’s first abolition in 1794 from progressive reinstatement during November 1802 to June 1804 and the later 1848 abolition. The May 1802 decree’s different effect in other colonies is not collapsed into a single simultaneous change everywhere. The source’s world-history uniqueness claim is not adopted.

Cherubini’s article abstract was read through its indexed text and used only for the 1809 to 1817 Portuguese occupation. Direct Érudit article and PDF access showed a challenge; the full article, original archival records and a separate 2022 book were not claimed as read. The 1817 return is not assigned an exact day or border settlement.

The 2020 Assembly report’s section 1(a) was read for the 1946 law and installation of territorial institutions on January 1, 2016. These are administrative transitions, not instant equality, universal citizenship or identical governance arrangements for interior communities. The account does not state that all colonial relationships ended in 1946. Electoral proposals, current officeholders and current legal advice are outside its scope.
The new narrative is author-checked and awaits independent historical review. No additional map coverage, successor relationship or polygon accuracy is certified.

proposedOverrides.summary: French Guiana is a territory of France in northeastern South America. Its history includes colonial administration, departmental status and the combined territorial institutions established in 2016.

identityEvidence.assessment: The outline depicts French Guiana in northeastern South America. Its imported 1878 to 2020 interval is map coverage, not a historical lifetime. The geographic card includes earlier named sites and later communities. It is not attached to Guyana, Suriname or the ambiguous broader Guiana entries. Geometry and coverage endpoints remain unchanged and unverified.
